record.paper_title: Progress in Nuclear Astrophysics: a multi-disciplinary field with still many open questions
record.context_brief: Reliable ML extrapolation for unknown nuclei
record.original_question: How can machine-learning methods be used in nuclear astrophysics so that they improve nuclear-data prediction or emulator efficiency without destroying predictive power when extrapolating to nuclei outside the training and validation region, especially heavy nuclei with Z ≥ 82? The paper reports that a neural-network test on masses truncated below Pb achieves good interpolation metrics inside the known region but produces an uncontrolled rms deviation of 37.8 MeV on the excluded heavy nuclei, and it therefore treats reliable extrapolation as an unresolved requirement even while arguing that ML can still be useful for reducing computational cost and scanning large model spaces.

evidence.quote: mass models in this way should be done with utmost care, since ML techniques inevitably add thousands of additional parameters. These will compensate for any model defects and aid in constructing accurate interpolation, but they might also reduce the predictive power when extrapolating to unknown nuclei.

Now, if we apply our latter algorithm to the 508 known masses for Z ≥ 82 nuclei, the rms deviation reaches a totally uncontrolled value of 37.8 MeV (with deviations up to 120 MeV for the heaviest nuclei known around Z = 110) on those 508 masses (and about 16.9 MeV globally on all the 2550 masses). This simple test shows that the ML extrapolation towards the heaviest nuclei excluded from the training and validation sets is uncontrolled.
Support from ML will certainly be more than welcome, but mathematics will not replace physics and special care should be given in their application to the extrapolation of data.

artifact.category_tag: Machine learning for nuclear mass prediction
artifact.status_search_result: Recent work (2024–2025) reports substantial progress on this question. Kernel ridge regression, convolutional neural networks with theoretical mass-model inputs (e.g., CNN-WS4), Bayesian/Gaussian-process emulators, symbolic regression, and physics-informed activation functions have all been proposed to improve extrapolation; some report rms deviations of order tens to hundreds of keV in the superheavy region and provide calibrated uncertainties. However, robust, universally accepted extrapolation with controlled uncertainty to the heaviest and drip-line nuclei remains an active and only partially solved research problem.

status_evidence.title: Robust extrapolation in nuclear mass predictions using domain-informed activation functions
status_evidence.snippet: Replacing standard nonlinear functions with physics-related activation functions significantly improves extrapolation performance.
status_evidence.claim: Physics-informed activation functions can substantially improve extrapolation robustness in ML nuclear mass models.

status_evidence.title: Nuclear mass predictions based on convolutional neural network
status_evidence.snippet: For superheavy nuclei (Z ≥ 104), the CNN-WS4 model predicts a deviation of 0.046 MeV from experimental masses.
status_evidence.claim: Hybrid CNN + theoretical-mass-model approaches achieve low rms deviation in the superheavy region, partially addressing the extrapolation issue.

status_evidence.title: Nuclear mass predictions using machine learning models
status_evidence.snippet: One of the most important issues in ML studies is low performance of models when extrapolating outside the training and test set regions.
status_evidence.claim: Extrapolation outside the training region remains a recognized open challenge in ML nuclear mass prediction.

status_evidence.title: Discovering nuclear models from symbolic machine learning
status_evidence.snippet: Symbolic ML approaches discover compact nuclear models with improved extrapolation behaviour.
status_evidence.claim: Symbolic regression offers a route to ML mass models with more controlled extrapolation.
